145.manipulation: Followed the egg's natural pigment 'zenith field' mark and added artificial marks, hair-ligature constrictions and punctures to uncleaved alpine-newt eggs.
145.design: Continuous observation of individually marked eggs through cleavage, with constriction and puncture interventions; results compared against the amphibian literature (Table β).
145.readout: Position of the embryo's median plane relative to the egg's mark and to the first cleavage furrow.
145.finding: Only 35 of 125 eggs had a symmetrical first furrow, presumably on the future midline; the animal-pole pigment spot, and punctures made there, ended at the embryo’s nape or crown.

38.manipulation: Castrated young rats and guinea pigs and implanted the opposite sex's gonad, or both glands together, to feminize, masculinize, or produce hermaphrodites.
38.design: Treatment animals versus normal controls; experimental sex reversal and induced double-sex ('hermaphrodite') glands.
38.readout: Development of secondary sexual characters, body form, mating behaviour, and gonad histology.
38.n: Series of implanted rodents (rats, guinea pigs)
38.finding: The gonad's interstitial 'puberty gland' secretes the hormones that determine secondary sex characters; implanting the opposite gland reverses or doubles them, yielding experimental hermaphrodites.

70.manipulation: Exchanged humerus and femur between newts (homoplastic grafts), or extirpated the humerus with the shoulder girdle, then amputated through the upper arm or thigh.
70.design: Comparison of regenerates from normal, out-of-place-skeleton, and skeleton-less stumps.
70.readout: Whether and how a correctly patterned limb skeleton re-forms in the regenerate.
70.n: Six X-rayed cases reported (two bone exchanges, four skeleton-less arms); total operated not stated
70.finding: Limb regeneration is independent of the pre-existing skeleton: the regenerate's skeleton forms anew from the blastema under a regional 'determination field'.

135.manipulation: Reared mantises from one ootheca at about 24.5–27 °C, weighing freshly moulted animals and their cast skins and measuring pronotum length at each moult.
135.design: Longitudinal measurement across successive instars; tabulation and fitting of growth curves.
135.readout: Pronotum length and mass of animals and cast skins at each moult, and the ratios between successive moults.
135.n: 38 mantises kept singly from the fifth moult, all from one ootheca; earlier moults measured on pooled larvae (10–16 per moult).
135.finding: Growth proceeds in regular stepwise ratios per moult — the empirical basis of what became 'Przibram's Rule' (~2.09x mass, ~1.26x linear dimension per instar).

39.manipulation: Kept midwife toads at 25–30 °C, which led them to breed in water without brood care; also varied moisture, removed eggs from males, prolonged larval life; bred descendants.
39.design: Control series versus descendant series across generations.
39.readout: Whether the enforced reproductive behaviour and associated structures reappear in the offspring.
39.finding: Kammerer reported that the environmentally enforced reproductive adaptations were inherited by the descendants — a Lamarckian claim, later disputed (the 1926 nuptial-pad scandal).

56.manipulation: Exposed green and brown hydra to CO2; starved and injected polyps; kept ovary-bearing green hydra in darkness or coloured light; halved immature eggs; tried to infect brown hydra.
56.design: Exploratory preliminary experiments and observations on Hydra biology.
56.readout: Survival, fate of injected material, algae in eggs and buds, egg development and hatching, size of halved oocytes, and algal culture on agar.
56.n: Five polyps per species and condition in the CO2 test; about 20 dark-reared eggs; 15–17 halved eggs; other trials not counted
56.finding: Green hydra withstood CO2 better than brown; in darkness or green light algae did not enter eggs, one of which still hatched; halved oocytes regained normal size; algae judged non-nutritive.

44.manipulation: Reared alpine salamander embryos removed from the uterus in water; kept captive alpine females with a water basin and fire salamander females without water; varied soil, temperature and moisture.
44.design: Comparative, statistical study across the two species and across conditions, with experimental induction of altered reproduction.
44.readout: Uterine contents (embryos, abortive eggs), stage and number of young at birth, larval gills and tail fin, coloration and spotting.
44.n: Large statistical series across both species
44.finding: Fire salamanders denied water came to bear few metamorphosed young; captive alpine females sometimes bore larvae; fire salamander embryo numbers fell with altitude; Kammerer inferred descent from a common ancestor.

93.manipulation: Kept normal and eye-amputated crustaceans (eyes mostly cut with the eyestalks) on coloured backgrounds, in daylight, darkness, night illumination, all-round sunlight and sudden temperature changes.
93.design: Series crossing background colour x light condition x intact/blinded animals; macroscopic and microscopic observation across the day-night cycle.
93.readout: Expansion and contraction of the chromatophores and the resulting body colour.
93.n: Four crustacean genera (Gelasimus, Potamobius, Palaemonetes, Palaemon)
93.finding: Most species showed a day–night colour rhythm; no lasting match to background colours was found; darkness or eye removal eventually bleached most species; eye-amputated crabs and crayfish moulted faster.

148.manipulation: Grafted supernumerary developed limbs onto amphibians and observed their innervation and movement.
148.design: Observation of the grafted limb's motor behaviour relative to the host's own homologous limb.
148.readout: Whether, and in what timing, the transplanted limb moves relative to the host's limbs.
148.n: 70 larvae with lasting grafts, mostly arm beside leg (29) or leg beside arm (28); nerve supply traced in sections of three
148.finding: Grafted arms regained function and moved simultaneously with the neighbouring host limb, muscle for muscle, whatever nerve branches supplied them; Weiss explained this by muscles ‘resonating’ to specific excitation forms.

9.manipulation: Removed the foot, split the lower leg between tibia and fibula, cut one half off near the knee, and covered the remaining half with skin from the removed half.
9.design: Preaxial or postaxial lower-leg half retained (left hindlimbs), or the forearm simply split (left forelimbs); regenerates from the distal and proximal half cross-sections compared.
9.readout: Whether a whole, correctly patterned limb regenerates from a partial cross-section.
9.n: 25 newts with clear results (14 preaxial, 8 postaxial, 3 split); operated June to August 1923
9.finding: 15 of 25 regenerates were whole (paired lower-leg bones, typical asymmetric foot), from one half cross-section and never both; 10 were partial or mosaic; ascribed to a limb field.

119.manipulation: Made alpine salamanders bear larvae (warmth, water) and fire salamanders bear metamorphosed young (no water) or lay eggs (heat); bred the altered-born young in outdoor enclosures.
119.design: Experimentally altered animals and their offspring compared against controls across generations.
119.readout: Whether the enforced reproductive mode and associated characters reappear in the offspring.
119.n: 26 late-born fire and 27 early-born alpine salamanders reared in outdoor enclosures; four fire salamander births and two alpine litters (3 and 5 larvae) reported.
119.finding: Kammerer reported that the experimentally enforced reproductive adaptations were transmitted to the offspring (a Lamarckian / atavism claim, later disputed).

81.manipulation: Injected minnows with adrenalin or posterior-pituitary extract (Infundin) at graded doses, alone or in sequence; compared with distilled water, ether, blinding, sympathetic-nerve section and black or yellow backgrounds.
81.design: Injected fish paired with matched controls on grey background and observed for hours; skin then fixed and chromatophore states examined by layer; Infundin first checked on frogs.
81.readout: Expansion and contraction of melanophores and xanthophores and the resulting colour.
81.n: Minnows from Lunz and Vienna, 7–64 per condition in Table I; a few loach, pike, crucian carp and roach; frogs for extract checks
81.finding: Adrenalin contracts melanophores but leaves xanthophores unchanged; Infundin expands melanophores, xanthophores and erythrophores, as in frogs, contrary to Spaeth; nervous and incretory factors jointly regulate colour change.

88.manipulation: Transplanted an eye onto a host salamander larva and followed the graft through metamorphosis.
88.design: Observation of the grafted eye's developmental timing relative to the host — a 'whole controls the part' test.
88.readout: Whether the transplanted eye metamorphoses in step with the host.
88.n: Series XIII and XV (12 three-animal experiments each) and XVIII (20 pairs), plus Series II–III of the first paper.
88.finding: Grafted eyes blacken their iris in step with host eyes, earlier on older hosts, later on younger, triggered from elsewhere in the body; larval end-stage combinations fall out of step.

11.manipulation: Tested what a regeneration blastema can form by placing tail-blastema material within the limb field in Triton.
11.design: Tail blastemas grafted onto forelimb stumps (mostly from another species, as a marker) versus own or same-species (unmarked) blastemas grafted beside the intact forelimb with a diverted brachial nerve.
11.readout: Whether tail-blastema forms limb structures when sited in the limb field.
11.n: Stump grafts: 7 gave limbs with tail-like appendages; beside-limb grafts: 11 developed, 9 evaluable (2 tail-like, 3 unorganised, 3 limb, 1 mixed)
11.finding: Stump grafts formed tail-like appendages on a host limb regenerate; 3 of 9 grafts beside the limb formed limb parts, which Weiss read as young blastema lacking preset organ identity.

164.manipulation: Grafted gonads, of one or both sexes, into castrated guinea pigs and rats; reported testis-implant operations on castrated men and on men described as homosexual; examined a goat’s ovaries histologically.
164.design: Three communications combining rodent graft results (citing repeats by other laboratories), reports of human operations, and histology of one goat with male-type sexual behaviour.
164.readout: Body and genital sex characters, sexual behaviour, and gonad histology.
164.n: Rodent numbers not stated; several human operation cases; two young female goats, one examined histologically
164.finding: Steinach concluded that male and female gland secretions antagonise each other, that dual grafts yield hermaphrodites, and that a hermaphrodite gland underlies homosexuality, citing operated men and a goat’s ovaries.

98.manipulation: Cut out eyes with surrounding skin and grafted each into the neck, beside the spinal ganglia, of another animal of the same species, mostly larvae, in three orientations.
98.design: Graft series on sighted and previously blinded fire-salamander larvae, near-metamorphic larvae, adults and alpine-newt larvae; grafts sectioned from 1 to 43 days, survivors kept a year.
98.readout: External state of cornea, lens and iris; histology of retina and optic nerve at intervals; survival per series.
98.n: About 100 grafts in five tabulated series, including six adults and eight alpine-newt larvae; 30% of 80 counted alive after a year.
98.finding: Grafted eyes lose visual cells, then regain typical retinal structure after several weeks without nerve connection, attributed to host nutrition; the optic nerve grows out, once into a spinal ganglion.

133.manipulation: In adult newts, extirpated whole legs, legs with their girdle, or both hindlegs with pelvis and adjoining vertebral segment; grafted limb pieces under flank skin; reinserted leg pieces reversed.
133.design: Extirpation series of increasing extent; autoplastic, homoplastic and heteroplastic graft series; a polarity-reversal series; outcomes checked by eye and X-ray over up to two years.
133.readout: Whether leg and girdle regrow after each extirpation; whether grafted pieces regrow distal parts, their toe number, movement and sensitivity.
133.n: Over 200 operated amphibians, chiefly Triton cristatus: 12 leg extirpations, 28 girdle removals, 8 spinal resections, 63 grafts, 7 reversals, with overlap between series
133.finding: Totally extirpated legs regrow; pelvis and legs regrow, from the vertebral column, even after removal of the whole pelvis, but not after vertebral resection; grafted pieces regrow distal parts.

170.manipulation: Took blood tyrosinase from caterpillars at pre-pupal stages and from pupae, pre-irradiated it in coloured boxes for varying times, varied its alkalinity, and exposed green pigment extracts to coloured light.
170.design: In-vitro series: stage-by-stage blood tyrosinase, sealed or open, pre-irradiated in white, black, yellow or darkness for two or four days, then tested on tyrosine in daylight.
170.readout: Blood colour and reaction by stage; onset colour and speed of melanin formation in tyrosine samples; fading or greening of green-pigment extracts.
170.n: Blood tyrosinase of caterpillars at three pre-pupal stages and of fresh pupae.
170.finding: Blood tyrosinase turns from alkaline to acid and is most light-sensitive in wandering larvae; after longer irradiation yellow exhausts it, black surroundings (ultraviolet) preserve it; yellow favours green pigment.

174.manipulation: Catalogued museum specimens and published cases of triplicated body parts and appendages across the animal kingdom, with their symmetry and signs of injury.
174.design: Comprehensive comparative survey plus analysis of the symmetry rule that governs triple formations.
174.readout: The geometry (mirror symmetry) and conditions of triple-limb formation.
174.finding: Triplications obeying Bateson symmetry rules occur throughout the Metazoa and arise by regeneration from the two surfaces of a break, not by mutation; the middle component mirrors its own side.

156.manipulation: Pre-irradiated tyrosinase extracts (mostly honey fungus, also insect and mammal) in coloured boxes, pre-warmed them or altered their acidity, then added them to tyrosine; tested animal chromogens and pigments.
156.design: Preliminary biochemical experiments on extracts as a first step toward the chemistry of colour.
156.readout: The colour-producing substances and their behaviour in extracts.
156.finding: Blue light first inhibits, yellow promotes tyrosinase, reversing with longer exposure; 40 °C pre-warming and alkali favour red, acid blue-violet; red pigment is a melanin intermediate; lipochromes are animal-made.

86.manipulation: Induced colour change in salamanders by rearing them on differently coloured backgrounds, then bred the colour-altered animals.
86.design: Offspring of colour-modified animals compared with controls across generations.
86.readout: Whether the enforced colour change reappears in the offspring.
86.finding: Kammerer reported yellow soil enlarging and black soil shrinking the yellow pattern; offspring showed the shift intensified if re-exposed, weakened on neutral ground; artificial-race hosts re-tuned transplanted ovaries.

59.manipulation: Reared larvae from five egg-packets in darkness, coloured light, coloured boxes, or on chlorophyll-free or etiolated food; applied electrical and tactile stimuli; amputated legs, including raptorial legs, at different levels.
59.design: Separate rearing series from each egg-packet testing light, light colour, food and background against a daylight control culture; amputation series at different levels; measurements at each moult.
59.readout: Green or brown colour at each stage; moult number; regeneration of amputated legs; lengths of thorax, femur, tibia and tarsi at each moult.
59.finding: Green and brown colouring was independent of light, food, background colour and electrical or tactile stimuli; raptorial legs regenerate like other legs; absolute growth rate appeared constant per individual.

92.manipulation: Kept olms above or below 15 °C, in daylight, darkness or red light, fed or starved; bred light-darkened animals; excised half an eyeball to test regeneration.
92.design: Altered-environment treatment versus the natural cave state.
92.readout: Reproduction, pigmentation, eye development and body reduction.
92.quantification: Semi-quantitative (tables of births, clutches and body measurements)
92.finding: Kammerer reported live birth below 15 °C and egg-laying above; light-induced dark pigment passed to offspring; light-reared young grew large eyes; starved olms shrank in length.

57.manipulation: Matured midwife toad and tree frog eggs on land or in water (Alytes also without paternal care); reared larvae in water or on land; varied light, temperature and food.
57.design: Experimental alteration of reproductive activity versus normal behaviour.
57.readout: Hatching stage, duration of embryonic and larval development, changes in larval gills, skin and pigment, survival on land and regeneration rate.
57.finding: Kammerer reported that land or water rearing, moisture, light, temperature and food shift hatching stage and larval duration; captive midwife toads sometimes spawned in water without brood care.

116.manipulation: Amputated tails of newts and Salamandra larvae and sectioned regenerates; grafted pigmented and unpigmented skin between sites or animals in tree frogs, newts, tadpoles, lizards, axolotls and mice.
116.design: Experimental and observational study of pigment formation.
116.readout: Origin and development of pigment in the skin.
116.n: Fifty mice grafted (four grafts took); tree-frog grafts followed for a year; other numbers not given.
116.finding: Branched pigment cells in tail regenerates arise from epidermal cells and migrate into the dermis; in lasting grafts, melanophores do not cross between graft and host skin.

165.manipulation: Examined, microscopically, the histological structure of the testis in a sample of men described as homosexual.
165.design: Histological description compared with the cryptorchid testes used as implants and a few normal testis preparations.
165.n: Testes removed at operation from five men (a sixth excluded); cryptorchid testes for comparison
165.finding: Reported atrophic tubules, fewer Leydig cells and large ‘F-cells’, read by Steinach as female puberty-gland cells and a diagnostic sign; he allowed they might occur in normal testes.

48.manipulation: Amputated parts of amphibian larvae of different ages, developmental stages and body sizes and assessed their regenerative capacity.
48.design: Comparison of regeneration across age, stage and size classes.
48.readout: Extent and rate of regeneration as a function of larval age, stage and size.
48.n: 655 animals of nine species in twelve experiments: 647 larvae (375 of them Rana temporaria) and 8 metamorphosed crested newts
48.finding: Anuran hindlimbs regrew while upper and lower leg formed an obtuse angle (Pelobates, Bombinator until metamorphosis); overwintered larvae at that stage did not; species size had no effect.

69.manipulation: Cut or removed the nerve supply of developed amphibian limbs and tested whether they still regenerate after amputation.
69.design: Regeneration of denervated versus innervated limbs.
69.readout: Whether and how the limb regenerates without its nerves.
69.n: 35 newts with main arm nerves removed (series M I–VI, N, two further cases) and 15 partial-denervation cases; opposite arm as control
69.finding: Removing the main arm nerves prevented regeneration and halted or reversed regenerates already forming; partial denervation only slowed it; Weiss judged the nerve action unspecific, a sympathetic “formative tonus”.

49.manipulation: Compared claw asymmetry in museum specimens of living and fossil decapods and amputated the large (K) claw of Xantho rivulosus males; reports earlier lobster and Alpheus regenerates.
49.design: Systematic survey across decapod families and fossil forms (Vienna, Munich, London collections), with amputation experiments at Trieste and a theoretical account of claw asymmetry.
49.readout: Claw form (massive K or slender Z claw), size, side, sex and coxa size per species; after amputation, which side forms the K claw.
49.n: Museum series across living and fossil decapod families; 20 Xantho rivulosus males operated (2 survived); two lobster regenerates figured
49.finding: Distinguished native from regenerative claw asymmetry; claw loss reversed it (Alpheus), was directly replaced (lobster) or gave equal claws (Xantho); asymmetry arose orthogenetically from equal claws, not through use.

125.manipulation: Amputated or extirpated legs, mandibles, wing rudiments or end segments, chiefly in larvae of 11 beetle species, and followed them through pupa to adult.
125.readout: Capacity and pattern of regeneration of beetle appendages.
125.n: Larvae of 11 species: Rhagium, Tenebrio, Lampyris, Platycerus, Oryctes, Cetonia, Hydrocharis, Hydrophilus aterrimus and piceus, Cybister, Dytiscus
125.finding: All 11 species regenerate; legs cut in larvae reappear at pupa and adult, smaller after later or deeper injury; Tenebrio and Rhagium larvae regrow legs as larvae, water-beetle larvae cannot.

159.manipulation: Kept pupating caterpillars on coloured backgrounds with eyes lacquered or cauterised, under graded light or added yellow or blue light, behind ultraviolet- or infrared-absorbing filters, and in a projected spectrum.
159.design: Treated groups compared with untreated controls from the same broods under matching light; filters interposed on one or two sides; quinine-sulphate filter against water and glass controls.
159.readout: Pupal colouration as a function of the surrounding light and background.
159.finding: Black gives darker pupae than darkness; lacquered-eye larvae still matched backgrounds, cauterised ones did not; yellow light greens and blue darkens pupae; the black effect attributed to reflected ultraviolet.

67.manipulation: Put caterpillars ready to pupate in ten coloured boxes (diffuse light or sunlight), darkness, a projected spectrum or graded white or yellow light; tested pupal blood and pigments chemically.
67.design: Background and light treatment series across pupae.
67.readout: Pupal colour type (light, middle, dark, green); blood tyrosinase reactions, chromogen and green pigment of each type; absorption spectra of extracts.
67.finding: Four pupal colour types arise: lightest on white, darkest on black, green on yellow-reflecting surfaces or in yellow light; types differ in blood tyrosinase and green pigment.

36.manipulation: Cut off an arm or leg of young fire-salamander larvae and wedged it, without sutures, into a needle hole beside or in place of the other same-side limb.
36.design: Morphological study of how the grafted limb takes and develops.
36.readout: Survival, healing and structure of the transplanted limb.
36.n: 81 larvae operated in five ways; 70 grafts healed in permanently, 3 animals died, 8 grafts failed.
36.finding: Grafted larval limbs healed in (70 of 81), grew, metamorphosed with the host and regained active movement, keeping their own form and pigment; arm grafts more often lost distal parts.

41.manipulation: Reared three generations at 17–37 °C; crossed colour types; amputated legs and bred from parents with regenerated tarsi; timed running at set temperatures; inseminated Sphodromantis females with Mantis religiosa spermatophores.
41.design: Starting from about 170 siblings of one egg-packet; colour scored at hatching and final moult across crosses; temperature and amputation groups compared with uninjured controls.
41.readout: Offspring colour ratios; tarsal segment number in offspring; moult number, pronotum growth and development time; running speed; Q10 values.
41.quantification: Quantitative (offspring counts, growth tables, Q10 values)
41.n: About 170 sibling Sphodromantis and their descendants over three generations; 2,605 offspring of operated parents counted for tarsal segments.
41.finding: Adult colour did not depend on 17–37 °C; crosses suggested brown dominant over green; regenerated four-segment tarsi were not inherited; Mantis sperm gave all-maternal Sphodromantis offspring (‘pseudogamy’).

110.manipulation: Experimentally manipulated the newts' gonads and observed the development of their secondary sexual characters (e.g., the breeding crest).
110.design: Comparison of secondary sex characters under gonadal manipulation versus normal.
110.readout: Development of secondary sexual characters in Triton.
110.n: 37 males castrated (20 survived for months) and 8 females (4 survived), plus regeneration and graft series
110.finding: Castrating adult males made crest, white tail band and head marbling regress within a year; castrated females were unchanged; crest regeneration weakened after castration; gonad grafts failed.

127.manipulation: Bred Angora cats and tracked the inheritance of asymmetric eye colour (odd-eyed cats) across generations.
127.design: Breeding crosses analysed for the inheritance pattern of eye-colour asymmetry.
127.finding: Eye-colour asymmetry was not always inherited as a unit: kittens were odd-eyed (same or reversed side) or had both eyes one parental colour; deafness followed the blue eye.

42.manipulation: Kept loaches on white, dark, mixed or coloured backgrounds in light or darkness, lit from above, below or through coloured glass; blinded one or both eyes; fed or starved them.
42.design: Seven experiments over two series (1907–09) comparing treated with normal or light-kept fish; blinded fish kept in light and darkness; excised skin placed on coloured underlays.
42.finding: Loaches match background shade and hue in light, even with one eye; fully blinded fish stay dark, pigmenting the belly only in light; hue matching attributed to light-converted black pigment.

149.manipulation: Exchanged developed fore- and hindlimbs of fire-salamander larvae by grafting (arm at the pelvis, leg at the shoulder), then amputated the grafts and followed their regeneration.
149.design: Regeneration tested on transplanted versus normal limbs.
149.readout: Limb type and digit number of the regenerate, its position, orientation and size, and its skin-spot pattern.
149.n: 36 larvae in the protocols; regenerates from 32 grafted stumps tabulated (16 arm, 16 leg)
149.finding: Arm stumps at the pelvis always regenerated four-fingered hands and leg stumps at the shoulder mostly five-toed feet; regenerate type, position and orientation followed the stump, not the site.

157.manipulation: No new experiments; builds a biochemical theory of animal colouration on the Part I extract results and published observations.
157.design: Theoretical synthesis applying ferment and chromogen sensitivities to protective colouration, aberrations, heredity, pattern, zoogeography and colour vision.
157.readout: The substances and mechanisms that produce animal colour.
157.finding: Proposes that light-, heat- and acid-sensitive ferments produce colour adaptation and aberrations, that parallel induction of germ cells forms colour races, and that colour vision works colour-photographically.

169.manipulation: Exposed animals (rats) to elevated temperature ('climate') and assessed the effect on the puberty gland and sexual maturity ('virility').
169.design: Constant-temperature chambers (25–40 °C) versus unheated stalls with seasonal temperatures; descendants returned to cooler rooms; human puberty data compiled from anthropological literature by climate and ‘race’.
169.readout: Leydig-cell counts, testis, accessory-gland and body size, age at first mating and fertility; in people, reported age at first menstruation.
169.quantification: Quantitative (cell counts, weights, fertility and menarche tables)
169.n: Leydig counts tabulated for 5 control and 10 heat-reared rats (3 descendants moved to cooler rooms); fertility records of 250 females; published human data
169.finding: Warm-reared rats had more Leydig cells, larger accessory glands and earlier mating, with the Leydig increase persisting in cooler-reared descendants; human puberty differences, including ‘racial’ ones, were ascribed to climate.

172.manipulation: Kept pupation-ready caterpillars on white or yellow grounds or in darkness with infrared or ultraviolet filtered out, dimmed light, warmth, cold or damp; bled caterpillars on yellow or black.
172.design: Control experiments isolating the spectral region responsible for pupal colour from confounding factors.
172.readout: Pupal colour as a function of the spectral region of light.
172.finding: Pale pupae on white attributed to heat rays: excluding infrared reduced opacity, warmth lightened, cold darkened pupae; bled caterpillars adapted normally, so blood loss did not explain eye-removal effects.

153.manipulation: Recalculated published quantitative regeneration data, and his own mantis-leg and fiddler-crab claw series, as size ratios of the regenerate between successive intervals or moults.
153.design: Literature synthesis: regeneration-velocity curves for 70 series from 20 species, compared with the mantis leg curve; postscript criticising Křiženecký.
153.readout: Rate and time-course of regeneration relative to growth.
153.n: 70 regeneration series from 20 species, mostly from other authors (Stockard, Zeleny, Morgan, Emmel, Durban, Ellis, Morgulis).
153.finding: Regeneration is, quantitatively, a temporary acceleration of normal growth — unifying the two processes.

167.manipulation: Cultured pure-bred lines of the ciliate Paramecium aurelia and measured body-size variation in relation to endomixis (periodic nuclear reorganization).
167.design: Biometry of size across the endomixis cycle within genetically pure lines.
167.readout: Body-size distribution and its variation through endomixis.
167.finding: Size means and variability cycle through each roughly four-week intermictic period; after each endomixis a line splits into sublines with different heritable mean sizes, which selection can maintain.

140.manipulation: Fixed mantises at successive moults and intermoult points; counted epidermal nuclei; measured ganglion nuclei, mesothorax ganglion, mesothorax, prothorax and eye facets on sections, animals and exuviae.
140.design: Animals fixed at successive stages for histology, with exuviae and live measurements; set up to test whether each moult is a whole-body cell-division step.
140.readout: Epidermal nuclei per unit length, ganglion nucleus size, mesothorax ganglion dimensions, and mesothorax, prothorax and facet dimensions at each moult.
140.n: 19 mantises from one ootheca (20 survivors of the hatch, one excluded).
140.finding: No mitoses seen; constant epidermal nucleus density implied cell number doubling per moult; ganglion, thorax and facet dimensions grew by the cube root of 2, with deviations near moult VI.

10.manipulation: Stripped the skin from crested-newt forelimbs, sheathed them in a donor newt’s everted lung as a skin substitute, then amputated within the lung-covered zone.
10.design: Traced whether regenerate skin derives from the surrounding old skin or from deeper tissue.
10.readout: Tissue source of the epidermis / skin on the regenerate.
10.n: 72 newts operated, 44 survived; three formed true regenerates, two examined histologically (a blastema and a four-fingered hand)
10.finding: Regenerate epidermis grew from the old epidermis, while its dermis, absent from the lung-covered stump, formed anew from the blastema; epidermis over lung formed glands without dermis.

73.manipulation: Grafted small rings of head- or foot-region tissue onto the head or foot end of another hydra, in original or inverted orientation; also cut hydras into five transverse pieces.
73.design: All eight combinations of ring origin, graft site and polarity, with head-to-foot and foot-to-head grafts as key tests; regeneration of pieces from five body levels compared.
73.n: 48 graft compounds (10 in each key series, 3–5 in the others); 10 hydras cut into five pieces each
73.finding: Head-region rings formed heads and foot-region rings feet at whichever end was free; mid-body tissue could form either, head potential falling aborally; the stock did not influence the graft.

141.manipulation: Coated the eyes of pupation-ready caterpillars with yellow or blue lacquer and kept them in neutral surroundings; set other caterpillars on Hering’s coloured papers or greys of equal brightness.
141.design: Yellow versus blue lacquered eyes in neutral surroundings; yellow, blue, violet and red papers each paired with a grey of equal brightness; grey terrarium and darkness controls.
141.readout: Pupal colour type (light, middle, dark or green; spotting, opacity) counted per condition.
141.finding: Yellow-lacquered eyes gave predominantly green pupae, blue-lacquered middle pupae; yellow papers gave green pupae, equally bright greys did not; the cue acts through the eye by hue.

158.manipulation: Sealed honey-fungus tyrosinase, alone or mixed with tyrosine, in air-free glass tubes, some pre-irradiated in coloured boxes; compared open, air-bubbled and carbon-dioxide samples.
158.design: Comparison of tyrosinase activity with versus without air exclusion.
158.readout: Persistence of tyrosinase, and so of pigment-forming capacity.
158.n: Two honey-fungus tyrosinase preparations, each as sealed and open samples in eight light conditions; further sealed tyrosine mixtures.
158.finding: Excluding air conserves tyrosinase — the melanin-forming enzyme is oxygen-sensitive and can be preserved anaerobically.

40.manipulation: Removed both eyes or only the lenses of young pike; exposed blind and seeing fish to dark or light backgrounds, light from below, darkness, and electrical or thermal stimuli.
40.design: Blinded fish compared with seeing controls kept under the same conditions, some blinded fish kept in darkness; repeated in different seasons.
40.finding: Blinded pike darken and stop responding to light but not to electrical or thermal stimuli; in light they grow belly pigment, in darkness pigment regresses; seeing pike pale in darkness.

60.manipulation: Compared form restoration after division, fusion or injury in liquid, flowing, swellable and rigid crystals with regeneration and morphallaxis in organisms, citing his own 1904 crystal experiments.
60.design: Theoretical essay, first part only: classification of equilibrium types, analogies drawn from published crystal work, and a critique of Driesch and other opponents of the analogy; long bibliography.
60.readout: Parallels in the restoration of proportional form after division, fusion or mutilation of crystals and organisms; growth and symmetry deferred to later parts.
60.finding: Crystals, especially liquid, flowing and swellable ones, restore proportional form after division or injury as organisms do; on this ground Przibram rejects the proofs of vitalism offered by Driesch.

64.manipulation: Measured rectal temperature of rats reared or long kept in constant-temperature chambers from 5 to 40 °C in 5-degree steps.
64.design: Readings taken at 5–6 p.m. by Uhlenhuth and Kammerer (1912–1914), by species, sex and age; suspect values excluded; compared with published rodent measurements.
64.readout: Rectal body temperature at each external temperature.
64.n: 38 individually numbered rats (M. rattus and albino M. decumanus), roughly one per temperature, species and sex; values mostly means of 10 daily readings.
64.finding: Rectal temperature rose with external temperature, about 0.75 °C per 5 °C from 5 to 40 °C, alike in both species; females ran about 0.5 °C warmer than males.

96.manipulation: Kept adult and near-pubertal rats and mice, and adult dormice, at about 5, 14–16, 25 or 33 °C, reared there or transferred, and took rectal temperatures.
96.design: Sets of mostly ten animals compared across room temperatures against a 16 °C reference; three weeks of habituation readings discarded, then readings on 4–5 days.
96.readout: Rectal temperature by clinical thermometer, averaged per set; genital-tissue temperature inferred, not measured.
96.n: Sets of 3–20 animals: adult rats and mice (mostly 10 per set), 5 dormice, near-pubertal rats (10 per set) and mice (3–4 per set)
96.finding: Adult rats reared at 33 °C were 1 °C warmer than at 16 °C; transferred adult rats and mice shifted 1.5–3 °C; rearing temperature did not affect near-pubertal animals.

138.manipulation: Grafted the external gills of fire-salamander larvae, with adjoining skin, into the nape of other larvae; the left and right gills of one donor went to two recipients.
138.design: Four series; in Series III donors and recipients came from litters of different ages, and graft resorption was timed against the host’s metamorphosis and the donor’s siblings.
138.readout: Timing of rapid resorption of the grafted gills relative to the host’s metamorphosis (own gill and tail-fin resorption, leaving the water); graft histology.
138.finding: Grafts show slow degenerative resorption, then abrupt resorption exactly synchronous with the host’s metamorphosis, whatever the donor’s age; the whole organism times gill resorption. No heterochronous case was seen.

21.manipulation: Kept pupation-ready caterpillars on coloured, metallic, black or white grounds, under coloured filters, with ultraviolet or infrared excluded, or with eyes removed or overpainted; assayed tyrosinase and blood acidity.
21.design: Light and background treatment series across several Vanessid species.
21.readout: Pupal colour versus light and background.
21.n: Vanessa io, V. urticae, Pyrameis cardui, P. atalanta pupae
21.finding: Vanessid pupae adapt their colour to light and background, extending the Pieris result to other butterflies.

107.manipulation: Cut antennae, tail bristles or the last abdominal segment of silverfish; in a jumping bristletail cut measured parts of antenna, palp and middle tail bristle and removed a leg.
107.design: Silverfish kept in jars (Vienna, 1904); Machilis kept singly in tubes (Roscoff), operated at 4–10.5 mm including sexually mature animals, with six unoperated controls.
107.readout: Moults, body length, and length of regenerated antennae, palps, legs and tail bristles; regeneration buds; moulting of unoperated mature controls.
107.n: Silverfish: 8 (segment), 6 (antennae) and some tail-bristle cuts; Machilis: 9 operated and 6 unoperated controls
107.finding: Antennae and tail bristles regrew fully, palps and legs less; sexually mature animals regenerated after moulting again, and an unoperated mature Machilis moulted, so moults likely continue after maturity.

108.manipulation: Mixed press-juice of octopus skin, eyes and muscle, squid eggs and olm skin with tyrosine and metal catalysts at varied temperature, light and aeration; kept olms in light or darkness.
108.design: Test-tube series with salt-solution, no-tyrosine and no-catalyst controls; eight olms kept a year in pairs under light or dark, with or without aeration.
108.readout: Darkening and black precipitate in the test tubes; pigmentation of the living olms.
108.finding: Melanin-forming tyrosinase occurs in cephalopod skin and eyes but not muscle, in unpigmented squid eggs and in olm skin; reactions needed metal catalysts; living olms pigmented only in light.

114.manipulation: Induced leg autotomy, or amputated or extirpated legs proximal to the autotomy plane (mantis forelegs through the femur), in larvae of six reared species; also removed cockroach wing rudiments.
114.design: Comparative regeneration of functionally distinct leg types during rearing.
114.n: Reared larvae of six species in several series per species; mantis forelegs: eight operated, one survived to regenerate
114.finding: All species regrew legs cut proximal to the autotomy plane, and mantis forelegs cut through the femur; grasshopper and field-cricket hind legs did not regrow after autotomy, cave-cricket legs did.

8.manipulation: Grafted lizard tail blastemas, lifted in the second or early third week after tail amputation, onto the site of an amputated forelimb whose humeral head was removed.
8.design: Heterotopic blastema grafts followed for months; graft-derived structures compared with the control tail regenerates at the donor stumps.
8.n: Not stated (heavy operative losses); 8 grafts formed tails, 6 examined in detail
8.finding: Most grafted blastemas did not develop further or formed small knobs; eight grew into curved, fully differentiated tails lacking spinal cord; none formed limb structures.

25.manipulation: Removed eyes and replanted them into the orbit without sutures (Przibram’s autophoric method), in fishes, amphibians and rats.
25.design: Replantation series across vertebrate classes, followed for weeks to months.
25.readout: Healing, survival, reflexes and behaviour of the replanted eyes; appearance of the fundus.
25.n: Series of crucian carp, newts, salamanders, frogs, toads and rats
25.finding: Reported that replanted eyes healed in and regained sight in fishes and amphibians, and in some rats.

111.manipulation: Removed both eyes of prawns; kept prawns in darkness, on white porcelain or on mirrors in strong light; cut the nerves to a leg; provoked vigorous leaping.
111.design: Blinded prawns followed for weeks to a year, with moult and eye-regeneration records, against normal prawns; begun at Roscoff (1905), repeated in Vienna on another species.
111.readout: Chromatophore expansion and contraction and the resulting colour change.
111.finding: Blinded prawns turn red-brown, then within weeks white (P. treillianus) or pale yellow (P. rectirostris); strong light and white ground contract chromatophores; explained as a nervous reflex from the eyes.

115.manipulation: No experiments: described abnormal collection specimens (Cucullia, Zygaena, Adela, Prionus, Cancer, three Nephrops) and compiled cases of homoeosis from the literature.
115.design: Specimen descriptions and a 17-row table of known cases, sorted into substitution, supernumerary and displacement homoeosis, from which rules were derived.
115.readout: Which part is replaced by which, and under what conditions.
115.n: Six numbered specimen entries (eight animals) plus literature cases
115.finding: Substitution homoeosis follows a rule: a less differentiated appendage, usually of a following segment (reversed for wings), replaces the original, probably through regeneration; supernumerary and displaced forms do not.

12.manipulation: Measured the body temperature of young brown rats and how it is shifted by the temperature of the surrounding world.
12.design: Body temperature recorded across a range of ambient temperatures.
12.readout: Body temperature as a function of external temperature.
12.finding: In 3.5-week-old rats, rectal temperature rose about 0.7 °C per 5 °C between 10 and 35 °C, as in adults; at 38–54 days females ran 0.74 °C warmer than males.

37.manipulation: Amputated arm and leg on one side of fire-salamander larvae and grafted one limb onto the other’s amputation site (arm to leg site or leg to arm site).
37.design: Orientation-matched arm grafts set exactly on the leg stump (6 larvae) versus leg grafts inserted obliquely near the arm stump (6); free amputation sites for comparison.
37.readout: Whether a regenerate formed at the grafted stump, its size and differentiation, and whether it displaced the graft.
37.finding: Grafts fitted exactly on the stump (4 of 6) suppressed its regeneration; obliquely placed grafts did not (6 of 6 regenerated), and regenerates pushed the graft aside in 4.

18.manipulation: Cut the hind leg mid-thigh, removed the lower shank with the foot, and pushed the remaining knee-piece, distal end first, into the skin sleeve over the femur stump.
18.design: One series of 16 metamorphosed crested newts, operated March–July 1912; outcomes described animal by animal from preserved specimens, sketches and X-rays about four months later.
18.readout: The axis along which the reversed limb regenerates or grows.
18.n: 16 crested newts; 7 died within days, 2 later; of 7 survivors, 4 formed double feet, 3 unclear.
18.finding: Inverted lower-leg bones regenerated a foot from their originally proximal end (polarity reversal); double feet arose where both lower-leg bones, or femur and implant, each formed a foot.

131.manipulation: Amputated second antennae, mostly the last two leg pairs, and the furca of individually kept water lice at set points in the moult cycle, some animals repeatedly.
131.design: Amputation just after first captive moult, on a later moult day, or at set fractions of the known intermoult, including just before the expected moult; unoperated moult records as controls.
131.readout: Days between successive moults (taken as growth rate), body length at moults, and progress of regeneration.
131.n: About 90 individually kept animals (1¾–11 mm) in the tables, plus young of one brood; moult records of 29 unoperated animals as controls.
131.finding: Moult intervals normally lengthened; amputation mostly shortened them during regeneration, but amputation later in the cycle first delayed the next moult, reconciling the opposite results of Emmel and Zeleny.

147.manipulation: Let moth and sawfly larvae spin on coloured grounds or in darkness, dry or moistened; tested cocoon extracts for DOPA; soaked silkworm cocoon strips in DOPA, tyrosine or catechol.
147.design: Cocoon colour compared across grounds and moisture; extracts of colour-variable (Saturnia, Eriogaster, Cimbex, Lophyrus) and invariable (Antheraea, Bombyx) cocoons tested; stored tyrosine melanisation samples checked for DOPA.
147.readout: Cocoon darkness; ferric-chloride, sodium-carbonate, silver-nitrate and alkali colour reactions for DOPA; tyrosinase tests with tyrosine.
147.finding: Moisture, not light or background colour, darkens cocoons through non-enzymatic blackening of DOPA in the silk; DOPA was absent from tyrosine melanisation, so tyrosinase presumably attacks the side chain.

160.manipulation: Kept midwife toads above 25 °C so they mated and spawned in water, then bred water-egg lines with and without continued warmth; castrated pad-bearing males; implanted testis tissue.
160.design: Multi-generation water-egg lines (to F6 in warmth, to F4 kept cool from F1) compared with normal land-breeding males; histology of thumb skin; castration and testis-implant controls.
160.readout: Presence, extent and microscopic structure of the nuptial pad on the male thumb and forearm; thumb skin of females.
160.n: Alytes lines from Appenzell and Harz stock to F6; two castrated F4 males; three normal males and three castrates given testis implants.
160.finding: Kammerer reported that from the grandchild generation on, water-bred males developed a nuptial pad that grew over generations and persisted to F4 without warmth; it cycled normally in castrates.

161.manipulation: Explanted leopard-frog iris and pigment-epithelium pieces into liquid or solid media; removed lenses from normal and transplanted eyes of fire-salamander larvae; sampled aqueous humour after lens removal in frogs.
161.design: Pigment behaviour of explants compared between liquid and solid media; serial sections of lentectomized and control salamander eyes; aqueous humour examined for free pigment.
161.readout: Pigment expulsion from explanted cells and fragments; the connective-tissue membrane around the iris and its gap after lens removal; free pigment in the aqueous humour.
161.n: 428 frog iris explants; 102 lens-regenerating and 38 control eyes of salamander larvae; aqueous humour from 19 lentectomized frogs
161.finding: Iris cells expel pigment mechanically in fluid media; lens removal tears a membranous iris sac, exposing the pupillary margin to aqueous humour, which depigments it and restores cell division.

168.manipulation: No experiments; theoretical conclusion of Part I, reinterpreting its iris-depigmentation results and earlier frog-skin wound studies without a stimulus concept.
168.design: Critical essay contrasting stimulus physiology with a physico-chemical method, using wound healing, iris depigmentation and gravity-induced forms (Herbst) as examples.
168.readout: None; argues from Part I results and the literature.
168.finding: Argues that wound responses such as iris depigmentation and skin-cell migration are purely mechanical, with cells passive, and that stimulus and irritability concepts should be dropped from biology.

50.manipulation: Cut out the upper jaw tip (intermaxillary), alone or with the lower jaw tip (symphysial part), in sand lizards; also amputated a hind toe in seven young.
50.design: Observation of jaw regeneration after excision.
50.readout: Extent and structure of the regenerated jaw.
50.n: 20 lizards in three series (4, 12 and 4), about 5–6 of which died; toe amputation in 7 young
50.finding: Jaw tips regrew within about three months, with lower-jaw teeth, but bore granular scales instead of a single shield and cartilage instead of bone; amputated toes did not regrow.

62.manipulation: Tracked rotifers and paramecia at 4-second intervals and measured paramecium spreading in a two-chamber diffusion apparatus, testing the Einstein relation between mean-square displacement and diffusion coefficient.
62.design: Track analysis against the relation for disordered movement (mean-square displacement proportional to time); diffusion coefficients from population counts compared with those from tracks.
62.readout: Ratios of mean-square displacement for doubled intervals; diffusion coefficients from animals counted per droplet; mean path velocity.
62.n: Hydatina: 5 animals tracked (15–49 points each); Paramecium: several track series and some 30 diffusion runs.
62.finding: Mean-square displacement roughly doubled with each doubling of interval in rotifers and paramecia; population diffusion coefficients matched tracking values; an apparent rise of D at high density was left unproven.

82.manipulation: No experiment; corrects a drawing error in Fig. e (p. 606) of Przibram’s 1924 limb-axis paper.
82.finding: The ‘homopleural DV’ circle in Fig. e showed a correctly inserted right-side graft instead of an inverted left-side one; readers are asked to reverse its pronged figure.

83.manipulation: Argued, in the light of experimental morphology, that external living conditions act as a cause of organic variation.
83.design: Synthetic / programmatic statement drawing the experimental evidence together.
83.readout: The link between external conditions and organic variation.
83.finding: External living conditions are presented as a driver of organic variation — the theoretical core of Kammerer's environmental programme.

84.manipulation: None new; re-examined published blastomere-isolation, regeneration and graft experiments, his own earlier Antedon results, and recorded malformations for evidence on the dorso-ventral axis.
84.design: Literature synthesis in four parts (egg blastomeres, regeneration, malformations, transplantation), asking in each whether dorsal and ventral parts can replace each other.
84.readout: Whether dorsal and ventral anlagen or body parts replace each other at full value after isolation, injury or malformation.
84.finding: Dorsal and ventral parts arise from separate anlagen that cannot replace each other at full value, in eggs or developed animals; each can form scarcely more than it normally forms.

94.manipulation: No experiment; set out a programme to measure whether eight external factors (chemicals, moisture, density, mechanical, gravity, electricity, radiation, temperature) reach the gonads through the body.
94.design: Work programme reviewing, factor by factor, how far each could penetrate the bodies of different animal groups; measurements assigned to named institute workers.
94.readout: None measured; proposed readouts are whether, and how strongly, each factor reaches the gonads and whether germ cells are shielded.
94.finding: Przibram treats inheritance of acquired characters as established and asks by what route; he argues the physical environment of the germ cells must first be measured.

97.manipulation: Kept blinded and seeing loaches in darkness 22–24 months; set blinded fish on white, orange or black backgrounds; grafted skin belly-to-back and between blinded and seeing fish.
97.design: Two series of blinded fish moved to coloured backgrounds at different delays after blinding; four graft types between regions or between blinded and seeing fish, observed up to ten months.
97.readout: Body colour by region over months; colour of grafts and spread of black pigment across graft borders (by eye and hand lens).
97.finding: Loaches, blinded or not, stayed dark in darkness for 22–24 months; blinded fish adapted only if moved soon after blinding; blinded–seeing grafts kept their colour for months, then were resorbed.

128.manipulation: Autotomized, denervated or totally extirpated the large claw, small claw or both, singly and in combination, in animals of different sizes; unoperated controls.
128.design: Regeneration of the paired claws after removal, tracking which becomes large.
128.readout: Which claw regenerates as the large versus the small form.
128.n: 20 species in 13 genera; 15 of 25 possible operation combinations carried out, mostly in Alpheus and Typton
128.finding: Claw reversal also occurs outside Alpheus, in Athanas, Typton, Callianassa, Carcinus and Portunus; it slows with size (transient two small claws above 10 mm carapace); nerve section only slows growth.

171.manipulation: Added tyrosinases (moth pupae, honey fungus), skin and eye press-juices, weak alkali or hydrogen peroxide to DOPA and tyrosine solutions; titrated extract acidity; tested chromogens with Millon’s reagent.
171.design: Tube series against untreated and alkali-only controls; albino versus pigmented rat skin and eyes; white, red-yellow and black guinea-pig skin; equimolecular DOPA and tyrosine dilutions.
171.readout: Speed and colour of blackening (initial colour, melanin precipitate); acidity of extracts by phenolphthalein titration and viscostagonometer; Millon’s reaction for tyrosine.
171.quantification: Semi-quantitative (titrated acidity; colours judged by eye)
171.finding: No separate DOPA-oxidase needed: DOPA blackens with weak alkali alone, and tyrosinase blackens equimolecular DOPA and tyrosine equally; acidity explains negative reactions in albino skin and eyes.

17.manipulation: Reared parthenogenetic stick insects from hatching in cages lined with 15 coloured papers, behind graded layers of coloured transparent paper, or in darkness; bred a second generation; blinded adults.
17.design: Adult colour types counted per cage at two dates in 1916; pooled and single-mother second-generation cultures kept in the same colours; histology, pigments and tyrosinase compared across types.
17.readout: Adult colour type (nine brown, red, black and green types); melanin and lipochrome content and tyrosinase activity of each type; percentage of offspring per type.
17.n: 464 first-generation adults from 35 cages of 15 young; 123 second-generation adults from pooled cultures, plus single-mother cultures
17.finding: Illumination sets colour type (light on pale, dark on dark or blue-violet surfaces, green in darkness); induced types increased in the second parthenogenetic generation; maternal colour also influenced offspring.

22.manipulation: Darkened fish by blinding, sympathetic-nerve section, air exposure, alcohol or ether, black background, darkness or killing; extracted melanin from equal-weight heated pieces of darkened and pale skin.
22.design: Comparison of melanin quantity between pale and dark states across species.
22.readout: Relative darkness of acid-precipitated melanin suspensions compared in paired test tubes and photographed; granule size and form under the microscope.
22.finding: The quantity of melanin itself changes during colour change — not only its distribution within chromatophores.

71.manipulation: Split lower leg and foot lengthwise and cut one half (tibial or fibular, with one to three toes) off at the knee, leaving longitudinal and half-transverse wounds.
71.design: Six operation types (T1–T3 tibial, F1–F3 fibular); regenerates from the longitudinal surface compared with those from the half cross-section at the knee.
71.readout: What regenerates from a lateral wound on the limb.
71.n: 112 newts operated; 36 gave clear results (T1 5, T2 6, T3 8, F1 7, F2 8, F3 2)
71.finding: Half cross-sections at the knee regrew whole feet; longitudinal surfaces did not restore the missing half but sprouted rows of separate toes, unless both blastemas fused early.

91.manipulation: Cut off the anterior 17–30 segments, including the whole genital region (segments 9–15), in about 300 Criodrilus lacuum; second, full communication.
91.design: Observation of how the genital apparatus is rebuilt after removal.
91.readout: Origin, number and segmental position of regenerated gonads, funnels, ducts, atria and sperm and egg sacs, in serial sections compared with normal worms.
91.quantification: Semi-quantitative (gonad counts and positions per worm)
91.n: About 300 operated worms; gonads counted in 28 and testes and ovaries in 23 sectioned regenerates
91.finding: Gonads arise anew from peritoneal cells on the septa; regenerates carried 4–12 gonads per side (normally 3), mostly more ovaries than testes, often in abnormal, more anterior segments.

100.manipulation: Crossed perch and ruffe by artificial fertilization in both directions, backcrossed wild-caught hybrid females to both parents, and reared hybrids and pure-bred controls under four temperature and culture conditions.
100.design: Reciprocal crosses and backcrosses with pure-bred controls, reared in parallel at about 10, 12–17, 16–18 and 25–30 °C; hybrids compared with both parent species.
100.readout: Hatching, growth in length over months, fin-ray and scale counts, body form and colour of hybrids versus parents; fertility of hybrid females.
100.quantification: Quantitative (growth tables at three temperatures; fin-ray and scale counts)
100.finding: Perch and ruffe can be hybridized, and the hybrids show an intermediate or distinctive character set.

117.manipulation: Exposed protozoa to seawater and recorded the effect on the pulsation of the contractile (pulsating) vacuole.
117.design: Contractile-vacuole activity in seawater versus fresh water.
117.readout: Rate or persistence of vacuole pulsation under raised salinity.
117.n: Four experimental series of isolated amoebae (numbers per series not stated), with control cultures
117.finding: Seawater slows or stops the contractile vacuole — the organelle's pulsation tracks the osmotic load, evidence of its osmoregulatory role.

51.manipulation: Cut away a piece of the right side of the head, with antenna and eye, in mealworm larvae and followed regeneration through moult and metamorphosis.
51.design: Observation of antenna and eye regeneration after excision.
51.readout: Presence and external form of the regenerates (antennal segment count, eye outline) after moult or pupation; no histology.
51.n: 23 larvae in two series (6 and 17); 2 survived with regenerates, one larva and one pupa that became a beetle
51.finding: Two survivors regrew antenna and eye; the beetle’s antenna had eight segments instead of eleven. The author announced eye regeneration, unknown in insects, pending histology.

65.manipulation: Removed the large claw, small claw or both by autotomy, or the large claw by total extirpation at the coxa, mostly in males; castration and testis grafts failed.
65.design: Operation groups of about five crabs with unoperated male controls; carapace and claws measured and claw form recorded at each moult, over several moults.
65.readout: Side and type (large or small) of each regenerated claw and its form at successive moults; carapace, claw and propodite lengths.
65.quantification: Semi-quantitative (carapace and claw lengths per moult)
65.n: 43 numbered crabs, most of them males, from about 100 shipped from Woods Hole; five unoperated male controls
65.finding: After autotomy the large claw regrew directly on the same side, confirming Zeleny; after total extirpation regeneration was delayed and passed through biramous- or walking-leg-like forms before becoming a claw.

129.manipulation: Removed the elytra, or elytra and hind wings, of adult mealworm beetles, following a chance find, in a mantis cage, of a feeder beetle whose removed elytra had regrown.
129.design: Observation of wing regeneration after excision.
129.readout: Extent and structure of the regenerated wings.
129.n: 33 adult beetles: 20 with elytra removed (one regenerated, rest died in 2–8 days), 13 with elytra and wings removed (all died); plus the chance find
129.finding: One of 20 adult beetles whose elytra were removed regrew elytra and hind wings from day ten, after its intact hind wings had shrunk away; a partial moult was suspected.

132.manipulation: Cut off the anterior 17–30 segments, the whole genital region, of about 300 medium-sized and adult Criodrilus lacuum; preliminary communication.
132.design: Observation of how the genital apparatus is rebuilt after removal.
132.readout: Gonads, ciliated funnels, seminal vesicles and male pores in serially sectioned regenerates, and their segment positions compared with normal worms.
132.finding: Regenerates formed ovaries, testes, funnels and seminal vesicles, often in extra, more anterior segments (ovaries in up to seven); somatic cells were inferred to become germ cells.

150.manipulation: Castrated adult newts and placed whole testes of another species, unsutured, in the body cavity (Pleurodeles and Triton species); also exchanged gonads between male and female crested newts.
150.design: Reciprocal testis exchange between Pleurodeles and two Triton species; in crested newts, testes into fully or partly castrated females and ovaries into castrated males.
150.readout: Graft histology (spermatogenesis, mitoses, degeneration), sperm in puncture fluid, and the hosts’ secondary sex characters.
150.n: Animal numbers not stated; hosts examined after 6 months (species exchange) or 1 year (crested-newt series)
150.finding: Whole testes grafted between species kept normal spermatogenesis for months (marbled-newt testes partly degenerated); hosts kept their own sex characters; testes also took beside a retained ovary.

154.manipulation: Cut Mantis religiosa forelegs through the femur; fractured Sphodromantis forelegs at the trochanter or femur end; cut antennae within the scape in older Sphodromantis larvae and nymphs.
154.design: Three series: foreleg regrowth, tested against Bordage’s negative claim; fracture groups of six at 25 and 35 °C; antenna cuts in nymphs kept near 17 °C.
154.readout: Regrowth of the foreleg; supernumerary parts at fracture sites; leg characters (femoral spines, tibial teeth, tarsi, claws) on antennal regenerates.
154.n: Three Mantis religiosa foreleg regenerates; 24 fractured Sphodromantis; six antennal regenerates in nymphs, two with leg ends
154.finding: Non-autotomizing mantid forelegs regenerate, contrary to Bordage; femur fractures gave supernumerary parts; antennae cut within the scape in nymphs regrew with leg characters, one with raptorial-foreleg spines and teeth.

4.manipulation: Took serial growth measurements of the Japanese mantis Tenodera aridifolia.
4.design: Longitudinal biometry of growth across instars.
4.readout: Weights of cast skins and of freshly moulted fasting animals; pronotum length and breadth per instar; moult number by sex.
4.n: 941 cast skins from 302 animals (1914 and 1928–29 broods); 18 live-weight quotients from animals weighed after moults 7–9.
4.finding: Weight about doubled per moult (skins 2.22, animals 2.19), with quotients rising in later instars; pronotum length rose 1.35-fold, not 1.26; sexes had equal moult numbers and similar size.

14.manipulation: Irradiated pupation-ready caterpillars on white, yellow or black grounds with a quartz lamp; compared filtered with reflected coloured light; used gold, silver and coloured metallic surroundings.
14.design: Light and background treatment series on Pieris pupae.
14.readout: Pupal colour versus light and background.
14.finding: Quartz-lamp irradiation darkened pupae on white or yellow, not on black; transmitted and reflected coloured light act alike; gold acts like yellow; black, red and yellow surfaces reflect ultraviolet.

20.manipulation: Tied a thread around the head of cabbage-white, peacock and small-tortoiseshell caterpillars and cut the head off in front of it, a heat-free alternative to cautery blinding.
20.design: Headless caterpillars kept on white, grey, yellow or black backgrounds; others decapitated only after suspending themselves, or ligatured without cutting; pupae compared with background and darkness types.
20.readout: Whether headless caterpillars pupate, the colour type of the pupae (light, medium, dark; white saddle in cabbage whites), and pupal form.
20.finding: Headless caterpillars pupated, up to two-thirds in some series, but gave medium pupae on every background: losing the eyes, not cautery heat, abolishes colour-matching, which is fixed once caterpillars suspend.

24.manipulation: Defined autophoric transplantation (graft held by the recipient’s own tissues, lids or pressure, without sutures), coined terms for graft combinations, and recounted earlier Antedon and rat-eye trials.
24.design: Methods and programme paper: definitions, history of the method, and proposed eye-graft problems (colour change, vision, species and class combinations) for the institute’s series.
24.readout: None; proposes later readouts such as body-colour change, vision, and colour and growth of grafted eyes.
24.finding: Autophoric grafts need no sutures, let vessels and nerves rejoin, and permit even cross-class (dysplastic) unions; eye replantation could open sense-physiology questions and might be tried on human eyes.

27.manipulation: Grafted eyes between species, e.g. a smooth-newt eye onto a young fire salamander, and followed their growth.
27.design: Heteroplastic eye grafts compared with the host’s own eyes.
27.readout: Size of grafted versus host eyes over time.
27.n: A few grafted newts and salamanders; replanted rat eyes
27.finding: A smooth-newt eye grafted onto a fire salamander grew only to newt-eye size, so the graft, not the host, set its growth.

28.manipulation: Sectioned replanted eyes from Koppányi’s operated animals at various intervals after the operation.
28.design: Histological examination of transplanted eyes in mammals and amphibians.
28.readout: Structure of retina and optic nerve in serial sections.
28.n: Replanted eyes of rats, a rabbit, newts and toads
28.finding: Described optic-nerve fibres regrowing towards the chiasma after eye replantation in rats and a rabbit.

55.manipulation: No manipulation: described malformed spiny dogfish donated by the Trieste zoological station, by external inspection, dissection and serial sections.
55.design: Descriptive case reports (Grosser), then a theoretical discussion of possible origins (Przibram), with an appeal for a developmental-mechanical museum.
55.readout: External form, skeleton, musculature, innervation and histology of each malformation, compared with normal specimens and published cases.
55.n: Five specimens: a half-grown 56 cm male, a 14 cm embryo, a near-term foetus and two double-headed embryos (14 cm and 26 mm)
55.finding: Described a nerveless head fin, gills on the upper jaw, a finless tail and two anterior duplications; Przibram suggested a displaced fin anlage, homoeosis, defect formation and separated cleavage cells.

78.manipulation: Applied ferric-chloride, sodium-carbonate and silver-nitrate colour tests for free DOPA to frozen sections of skin, eyes, plant tissue, cocoons and pupae, for comparison with earlier extract tests.
78.design: Sections of Bloch’s objects (rat, rabbit and human skin; rat eyes) alongside DOPA-positive (broad bean, Saturnia and Eriogaster cocoons) and DOPA-negative (silkworm cocoon) controls.
78.readout: Green colour with ferric chloride turning purple-red with sodium carbonate, and silver-nitrate blackening, seen microscopically on the sections.
78.n: Sections from young and adult rats, a rabbit, human embryos and adults; broad-bean, cocoon and butterfly-pupa controls
78.finding: Sections showed free DOPA where extracts had (broad bean, Saturnia and Eriogaster cocoons) but none in rat, rabbit or human skin or rat eyes; sections and extracts agree.

85.manipulation: Cut off one eye of narcotized cockroach and mealworm larvae and destroyed the underlying optic ganglia with a hot needle or by a deep cut.
85.design: Two operative methods in Stylopyga larvae (cautery, deep cut) and deep excision in Tenebrio larvae; survivors followed through their moults to the adult.
85.readout: The form of the structure regenerated where the eye had been.
85.n: 312 cauterized and about 200 cut cockroach larvae (4 and 15 survived); Tenebrio numbers not given; outgrowths in two cockroaches and one beetle
85.finding: Two cockroaches and one mealworm beetle formed unpigmented, barely jointed, bristle-tipped outgrowths where the eye had been, described as antenna-like; others healed or regrew small eyes.

99.manipulation: Cut off the right tentacle of Planorbis corneus, Limnaea stagnalis and Paludina vivipara (in males the penis-bearing tentacle) and an eye-bearing tentacle of the slug Limax arborum.
99.n: 24 Limax arborum; Planorbis, Limnaea and Paludina series (mature and young males, females) not counted
99.finding: Planorbis regrew cut tentacles within two months; Limnaea stagnalis did not within three; Paludina males regrew a slender tentacle holding a blind penis rudiment; Limax regrew tentacles with eyes.

106.manipulation: Reared larvae in natural green or brown surroundings, moist or dry air, at 17, 27 or 37 °C; exposed cold-reared larvae to direct sun; amputated raptorial forelegs.
106.design: Ten of twelve combinations of surroundings, humidity and temperature, with control cultures at 22–25 °C; larvae from several egg-packets kept in groups.
106.readout: Colour change and regeneration of amputated parts.
106.finding: Colour was unaffected by green or brown surroundings and humidity; reared adults were mostly yellow, which he called a captivity colour; cold larvae greened briefly in sunlight; forelegs regenerate.

112.manipulation: Measured how the size of eggs and of newborns increases with the advancing age of the mother.
112.design: Comparison of eggs and young from larger (presumed older) and smaller mothers in frogs, perch, salamanders and turtles; successive broods of captive salamanders; four perch crosses varying parental size.
112.readout: Egg length and breadth; length of hatchlings, larvae and newborns; larval number and abortive eggs per brood in fire salamanders.
112.n: Frogs: 4 females per species; perch: 4 crosses; wild salamanders: 35 mothers; captive salamanders: 5 of 50 reported cases tabulated, 5–11 births each; turtles: 2 per species.
112.finding: Egg and newborn size rise with the mother's age — a maternal-age effect on offspring size.

130.manipulation: Removed the wing of an adult fly (imago) and tested whether it regenerates.
130.design: Observation of wing regeneration in the adult dipteran.
130.readout: Whether the adult fly wing regrows.
130.n: Probably thousands of house flies and blue blow-flies operated; five regenerates (one Musca domestica, four blow-flies)
130.finding: Fore-wings torn out of freshly emerged flies regrew in five cases without a moult, by inflation of a wound membrane; amputation, or operation on older flies, gave only wound healing.

134.manipulation: Starved juvenile crested newts for about 7–8 weeks and then refed them, fed others intermittently, and amputated tails in fed and starving newts.
134.design: Five series of 16 individually kept newts, each in four groups of four: fed controls, starved then refed, intermittently fed, regenerating fed, regenerating starved.
134.readout: Body weight, body and tail length, mostly weekly; tail regenerate length; food eaten and retained after refeeding in some animals.
134.n: 80 juvenile Triton cristatus: five series of 16, each animal kept singly.
134.finding: Refed starved newts gained weight 1.6 to 2.5 times faster than controls on half the feedings; intermittently fed newts stayed smaller; an internal growth drive, not food supply, governs growth.

143.manipulation: Cut the right antenna through the flagellum or through the two-segmented shaft at hatching, the 6th–7th moult or the penultimate moult; some leg-like regenerates were cut again.
143.design: Cut level (flagellum or shaft) crossed with larval stage; leg-regenerates re-amputated; antenna-legs tested with touch, alcohol and electrical stimuli against normal antennae and legs.
143.readout: Regenerate type at the imago (antenna, leg-like, none) and its segments; responses of antenna-legs to touch, alcohol and electrical stimulation.
143.n: 131 hatchlings cut in the shaft, 9 in the flagellum; 20, 29, 12 and 31 cut at later moults; 13, 7 and 8 leg-regenerates re-cut
143.finding: At hatching, flagellum cuts regrew antennae and shaft cuts gave leg-like regenerates (41%) or none (49%); later shaft cuts regrew nothing or buds; antenna-legs reacted to stimuli like antennae.

43.manipulation: Removed beak tissue from the domestic goose and duck and followed its regeneration.
43.design: Observation of beak regeneration in two waterfowl.
43.readout: Extent and structure of the regenerated beak.
43.n: 5 geese (3 cut near the nostrils, 2 by about 4 mm) and 8 ducks (5 and 3), all about three weeks old; 3 ducks died early; 5 sectioned
43.finding: Beak tips cut from three-week-old geese and ducks of both sexes regrew, mostly completely, within 4–6 weeks, with epithelium, bone, connective tissue and tactile corpuscles but apparently no glands.

54.manipulation: Amputated the fins of European freshwater fishes and followed their experimental regeneration.
54.design: Observation of fin regeneration across species.
54.readout: Extent and pattern of fin regrowth.
54.n: 41 fish of seven species at the end, 1–6 per fin and species (pectoral, dorsal or tail fin)
54.finding: Tail fins regrew in every species tested, dorsal fins partly, pectoral fins not; regrown fins restored their markings; the author judged capacity greatest along the body’s long axis.

74.manipulation: Reared rats at different temperatures and measured the resulting tail length.
74.design: Tail length as a direct function of rearing temperature.
74.finding: Relative tail length rose with rearing temperature (5–40 °C): the body:tail index fell about 0.037 per 5 °C, alike at 2 and 7–8 weeks; humidity had no decisive effect.

109.manipulation: Cut one hind leg at the coxa–trochanter joint in lab-hatched water spiders, kept in their usual water, clean spring water or on moist filter paper; needle-injured legs to test autotomy.
109.design: Comparison of keeping conditions after amputation, with transfers between water and moist paper; autotomy observed after injury; minnows offered water spiders as prey.
109.readout: Survival, regeneration buds and regenerated legs at later moults; time to autotomy after leg injury; minnows’ acceptance of spiders.
109.n: Not stated: young from several laboratory matings; ‘some’ regenerated; autotomy seen in ‘several’ spiders
109.finding: Hind legs regenerated only in spiders kept out of water and not past their second moult; regenerates were small but normally segmented; autotomy followed leg injury after hours.

146.manipulation: Analysed the axis-relations and developmental potencies of urodele limbs with models built to interpret Harrison's transplantation experiments.
146.design: Model-based analysis of how the limb's axes and potencies are arranged.
146.readout: The arrangement of limb axes and the potencies along them.
146.finding: Argued that Harrison’s reversed-symmetry limbs arose from the graft’s own potencies, by mirror-image outgrowth from its proximal wound surface, not from retuning by the host body.

3.manipulation: Removed the proximal or distal half of one long bone (humerus, radius, ulna, femur, tibia or fibula) through a small incision, cutting mid-shaft and leaving the limb intact.
3.design: All twelve bone-and-half combinations in two series (1924, 1926); regrown bones examined months later by dissection, serial sections or X-ray.
3.readout: Whether and how the long bones rebuild.
3.n: 108 operations on 73 newts (53 in 1924, 20 in 1926): 38 distal-half and 70 proximal-half removals
3.finding: Proximal halves regrew the missing distal half typically (all 22 regenerates); distal halves regrew mirror images of themselves (23) or atypical forms (13), never the proximal half.

5.manipulation: Measured the increase in the size and number of compound-eye facets as the mantis Sphodromantis grows (fourth growth-measurement communication).
5.design: Hatchlings compared with their adult mother (ten moults), combined with earlier exuviae facet data and section counts by Friza; comparison with Dixippus and other hemimetabolous insects from the literature.
5.readout: Facets per eye row on photographs and per section, facet length by photographic size matching, eye and head diameter, hatchling versus adult.
5.n: One mother and hatchlings from one of her oothecae photographed; Friza section counts on 6–7 hatchlings and 2–3 adult females; earlier moult data reused.
5.finding: Facet number doubled and facet length rose 3.8-fold from hatchling to adult; length grew 1.26-fold per moult except stages VI–IX, when number doubled; doubling not primarily due to cell division.

16.manipulation: Reared fire-salamander larvae against yellow versus black surroundings and scored the spot pattern of the resulting adults.
16.design: Adult spot pattern as a function of the larva's background colour.
16.readout: The black-and-yellow spot pattern of the adult salamander.
16.quantification: Qualitative (drawn patterns compared by eye; light intensity measured)
16.finding: The colour of the larva's surroundings influences the adult salamander's spot pattern — environmental determination of a 'fixed' colour pattern.

34.manipulation: Removed the lens of adult fishes and anurans through a corneal slit and set it, without sutures, into the same eye or one of another individual, species or class.
34.design: Series in fishes (autoplastic, homoplastic, heteroplastic, replacement of cataractous lenses) and in two anurans, plus a few fish-to-frog grafts; animals kept to autumn or winter.
34.readout: Whether the replanted lens survives and stays functional.
34.n: 145 fish transplantations listed, 13 of them cataract replacements; 22 successful anuran grafts; two successful fish-to-frog grafts.
34.finding: Unsutured lens grafts healed and stayed functional in fishes and anurans, auto-, homo- and heteroplastically; fish-to-frog grafts succeeded twice; healthy lenses worked in crucian-carp eyes that had cataract.

47.manipulation: Cut off the first segment, two or more anterior segments, or one to three antennae with their part of the first segment in Ophryotrocha puerilis; some wounds held open.
47.readout: Rebuilding of the worm's anterior end.
47.n: 24 animals in the regeneration table (1–9 per cut); wholly negative series, including held-open wounds, not tabulated
