47.finding: No regeneration after loss of two or more segments (jaw apparatus expelled, eyes not regrown); after first-segment loss, segment two sometimes grew antennae; antennae with first-segment parts regrew within days.

52.manipulation: Cut off the upper jaw tip up to the nostrils, often with the lower jaw tip, in lizards, geckos, newts and frogs; removed the horny beak of tadpoles.
52.design: Comparison across species (eight with results) and, within frogs, between tadpoles, small and large animals; dated protocols, cross-sections and maceration.
52.readout: Extent and structure of the regenerated jaw.
52.n: 161 animals in eleven tabulated series (7–26 each); further Lacerta vivipara and L. viridis, number not given
52.finding: Newts regrew jaw tips fully, bone and teeth included; tadpoles and small frogs did, large frogs not; lizards and geckos regrew them without bone and with altered scales.

63.manipulation: Measured the rates of the mantis's vital processes at different temperatures and computed their temperature coefficients.
63.design: Physiological rates across a temperature range, expressed as temperature quotients.
63.readout: The Q10 / temperature coefficients of life processes.
63.finding: Egg and moult development doubled in speed over 25–35 °C (Q10 about 2); egg Q10 was 1.2 over 30–35 °C, 6.3 over 20–25 °C; alternating 35/25 °C equalled 30 °C.

66.manipulation: Amputated the antennae of half-grown Sphodromantis mantis larvae and followed their regeneration.
66.design: Observation of antenna regeneration at a defined larval stage.
66.readout: Whether and how the antenna regrows, and in what form.
66.n: 87 sibling larvae operated just after the fifth moult at 25 or 35 °C; 44 reared to the adult
66.finding: No distinct leg parts formed: cuts proximal to the flagellum gave malformed regenerates with at most superficial foot-like features; cuts within the flagellum regrew normal antennae.

72.manipulation: Measured the angles of the venation / form of the butterfly wing.
72.design: Methods paper: descaled wings contact-printed on photographic paper; vein angles set with a mirror and read on a crystallographic goniometer; preliminary tables for two species.
72.readout: Branching angles between wing veins in left and right fore and hind wings, averaged over three readings.
72.n: Vanessa (Aglais) io: 21 fore and 15 hind wings; Aporia crataegi: 11 fore and 10 hind wings.
72.finding: Angles measured to about one degree varied between individuals and between left and right wings; species differences in some angles traced to the obliterated Media vein.

79.manipulation: Tested hot-water extracts of skin, scales and hair for free DOPA (ferric chloride, sodium carbonate, silver nitrate) and deproteinised fish-skin and pupal extracts for free tyrosine (Millon’s reaction).
79.design: Pigmented and unpigmented areas of young and adult animals; DOPA dilution series to set test sensitivity; albumin–tyrosine mixtures to check tyrosine loss during protein removal.
79.readout: Green colour with ferric chloride turning purple-red with sodium carbonate; silver-nitrate blackening; Millon’s reaction before and after protein removal.
79.n: Skin and skin-covering extracts from 11 vertebrate species; tyrosine tests on 4 crucian carp, 5 roach, 9 Sphinx and 15 Phalera pupae
79.finding: No DOPA reaction in any vertebrate skin or skin-covering extract, so DOPA is not the usual chromogen; tyrosine tests inconclusive, since protein removal carries tyrosine down; tyrosine remains possible.

1.manipulation: Excised from newt hind legs the fibula with its surrounding region (with or without toe 5), the fibular tarsus with toe 5, the whole fibular side, or toe 5 alone.
1.readout: What regenerates from a leg cut back only along one edge.
1.n: 50 newts, 10 per operation series (B–F); 43 examined, some later poorly fed
1.finding: Fibula excised with its region: restored as a fibula-like bone in over half the cases, else replaced by a knee regenerate with one lower-leg bone; triple formations also arose.

2.manipulation: Severed a newt arm above the elbow, removed the hand, and drew the piece crosswise through a tunnel bored through the trunk, leaving both cut ends exposed.
2.design: Regeneration at the proximal- and distal-facing cut ends compared in adults and larvae; side and axes of regenerates judged against the implant and the host side.
2.readout: The symmetry and completeness of the regenerate.
2.n: Two adult newts with regenerates described (T 118, T 508); two Triton taeniatus and two Salamandra larvae; total operated not stated
2.finding: Adults regenerated only from the proximal-facing end, larvae only from the distal end; proximal regenerates mirrored the implant, distal ones kept its side; the host body did not set symmetry.

6.manipulation: Mutilated newt legs along the tibial edge or medially, and noted a heteromorphosis of the long bone after excision of the fibular edge.
6.design: Regeneration across different edge-restricted mutilations, with attention to bone heteromorphosis.
6.readout: Regenerated structures and abnormal (heteromorphic) long-bone forms.
6.n: About 130 newts in 13 Sciacchitano series of 10; Weiss series of 16–26 newts, many without results; the long-bone heteromorphosis is one newt (no. 170)
6.finding: Excised tibiae did not regrow within two months; triplications arose only where a proximal-facing wound lay between distal-facing ones; one newt grew an apparently mirrored tibia instead of a fibula.

7.manipulation: Excised the posterior or anterior closing plate, or the whole first thoracic spiracle, in young nymphs; excised eyes with or without the optic ganglion; also described untreated abnormal specimens.
7.design: Spiracle-operation series followed through moults to the adult; eye-excision groups with the ganglion kept or removed; natural leg and antenna abnormalities compared.
7.readout: The aberrant structures formed at spiracles and elsewhere.
7.n: Spiracle: 17 nymphs (posterior plate), 3 (anterior plate), an earlier whole-spiracle series; 88 operated eyes; untreated specimens with leg and antenna abnormalities
7.finding: Posterior closing plates regrew as mirror-image anterior plates, or not at all; anterior plates and whole spiracles did not regrow; spiracle-like head openings came from a displaced mandibular tendon.

13.manipulation: Lowered the body temperature of young rats by chemical means and measured the effect on tail length.
13.design: Tail length under chemically lowered body temperature versus normal.
13.readout: Tail length as a function of lowered body temperature.
13.finding: Quinine or antipyrine injections lowering body temperature by 2–3 °C reduced relative tail growth over 9–11 days versus littermate controls, most clearly with antipyrine at 15 °C; fever induction failed.

15.manipulation: Reared fire-salamander larvae from birth to metamorphosis under yellow, blue or violet liquid-filled bells, colourless bells, uncovered or in darkness; some in dilute salt solution.
15.design: Five experiments splitting broods among coloured, colourless and dark cultures; salt solution combined with yellow or violet bells; black chromatophores counted in skin whole-mounts from selected cultures.
15.readout: Extent of yellow and black at metamorphosis, judged by eye; numbers of expanded and contracted black chromatophores per microscope field.
15.quantification: Semi-quantitative (chromatophore counts; patterns judged by eye)
15.finding: Transmitted yellow light gave yellower, dark violet or dark blue light blacker salamanders at metamorphosis; colour quality, not intensity, decided; yellow cancelled salt blackening; expanded chromatophores multiplied.

19.manipulation: Amputated the right foreleg between trochanter and femur in nymphs; in Sphodromantis, first punctured the thoracic ganglion with a hot needle or cut the coxal nerve.
19.design: Amputation series in two genera not tested before; in Sphodromantis, ganglion-punctured limbs compared with amputation-only, nerve-cut and unoperated controls; followed through moults.
19.readout: Extent and pattern of foreleg regeneration.
19.n: Parathenodera 12, Stagmomantis 10 and 9 nymphs; Sphodromantis 60 and 33 in ganglion-puncture and control sets; heavy losses
19.finding: Forelegs of Parathenodera and Stagmomantis nymphs regenerated as miniatures, often with fewer tarsal joints, contrary to Bordage; ganglion punctures failed as movement returned, and no less-differentiated limbs appeared.

23.manipulation: Reviewed English-language works on quantitative biology that reached Vienna after the wartime scientific blockade: two books by Loeb, the Journal of General Physiology, D’Arcy Thompson (1917) and MacLeod (1919).
23.design: Five short reviews (Referate), largely quoting the authors, with a closing comparison of their aims.
23.readout: Summary of each work and a comparison of how the three authors use quantitative biology.
23.finding: Loeb, D’Arcy Thompson and MacLeod use quantitative biology for different ends; all three deny special adaptation and reject crystal analogies, which the reviewer says does not follow from their views.

26.manipulation: Replanted rat eyes into the orbit by the suture-free method and followed the animals for months.
26.design: Case histories of operated rats with reflex and behaviour tests.
26.readout: Pupil and other reflexes, behaviour, and the state of the replanted eye.
26.n: About thirty rats operated in 1922; two eyes judged functional
26.finding: Reported that some replanted rat eyes regained optic pupil reflexes and visually guided behaviour.

29.manipulation: Grafted eyes between differently coloured animals and into blinded animals, in the orbit or on the neck.
29.design: Colour-contrasting eye grafts in amphibians and a fish.
29.readout: Iris and fundus colour of the grafts; body colour change of blinded hosts.
29.n: Small series of newts, axolotls, salamanders and crucian carp
29.finding: Grafted eyes changed colour from within rather than by pigment immigration; orbital but not neck grafts restored blinded hosts’ colour change.

30.manipulation: Trained rats with replanted eyes, blinded rats and normal rats to choose between optically different vessels.
30.design: Discrimination training with daily choice records for every rat.
30.readout: Correct and wrong choices over training days.
30.n: Two rats with replanted eyes, with blinded and normal controls
30.finding: Rats with replanted eyes learned brightness discriminations that blinded rats did not.

31.manipulation: Cut off insect heads and replanted them on the same or another individual, within and between species.
31.design: Head replantation in water beetles and other insects, followed for days to weeks.
31.readout: Healing, swimming, feeding and faeces of the operated animals.
31.n: Hydrophilus and Dytiscus beetles; Notonecta, Dixippus, Tenebrio larvae and Vanessa pupae
31.finding: Reported that exchanged heads healed on and regained full function, judged by swimming, feeding and dyed faeces.

32.manipulation: Exchanged heads between male and female Hydrophilus beetles.
32.design: Cross-sex head exchange with observation of mating behaviour.
32.readout: Mounting and courtship behaviour of the operated beetles.
32.finding: Females carrying male heads mounted females, while males carrying female heads stayed passive.

33.manipulation: Transplanted heads between differently coloured insects.
33.design: Head grafts in water beetles, water bugs, stick insects and mealworms.
33.readout: Body colour of the recipients after grafting.
33.n: Hydrophilus, Dytiscus, Notonecta, Dixippus and Tenebrio
33.finding: Reported that a transplanted head imposed its colour on the recipient’s body through its eyes.

35.manipulation: Placed whole ovaries, without sutures, inside the uterus of pregnant or just-delivered rats; mostly ovaries from other rats (homoplastic), in a few the animal’s own.
35.design: Hosts with or without own ovaries removed; albino hosts mated to albino males received ovaries from pigmented donors, so coat colour of young showed graft origin and host influence.
35.readout: Litters from grafted females, coat colour of the young, and litter size.
35.n: 7 autografted and 68 homoplastically grafted females (32 keeping their own ovaries); 14 hosts without own ovaries bore litters
35.finding: Uterine ovary grafts yielded litters; homoplastic grafts did so only when the host’s ovaries were removed; pigmented young from albino hosts showed graft origin; no host influence on the young.

45.manipulation: Tore out the entire third left maxilliped, with its basal segments and gill, in small crayfish (3–4½ cm) and followed regeneration for about 2½ months.
45.readout: Extent and form of the regenerated maxilliped.
45.n: 100 crayfish set up; 15 survived to the end: 7 regenerated, 8 (not yet moulted) showed none
45.finding: After total extirpation the third maxilliped regrew with its gill; intermediate stages resembled walking legs more than in crabs, which the author ascribed to the crayfish’s lower phylogenetic position.

46.manipulation: Cut off tentacles of Planorbis corneus and Paludina vivipara; in Paludina of both sexes the right tentacle, which in males carries the penis.
46.n: Not stated (a series of Paludina of both sexes; Planorbis number not given)
46.finding: Planorbis regrew cut tentacles quickly and Paludina within a few months, against Carrière’s negative result; in males the regrown right tentacle lacked the club-shaped, penis-bearing thickening.

53.manipulation: Tested the regenerative capacity of the lancelet Amphioxus lanceolatus after amputation.
53.design: Observation of regeneration in a basal chordate.
53.n: 12 lancelets (2–3½ cm) operated; 10 died of infection; 2 survived 25 weeks
53.finding: Of two survivors, one regenerated the anterior end and one only closed the wound; the author inferred a relatively slight regenerative capacity, against Nusbaum’s negative result.

58.manipulation: Inverted two freshly spun Hydrophilus aterrimus cocoons, fixed by their algal tuft, reversing the eggs’ orientation to gravity and lifting the former underside out of the water.
58.design: Two inverted cocoons compared with two upright control cocoons spun a day earlier and a day later; water about 10 cm deep, about 22 °C.
58.readout: Hatching date, number of hatched larvae, larval length, behaviour and survival, and the larvae and embryos left in the cocoon, including their orientation.
58.n: Two inverted and two control cocoons; controls hatched 28 and 42 larvae, inverted cocoons 3 and 5.
58.finding: Inverted cocoons hatched late, giving few small larvae that soon died and leaving many stunted larvae and embryos; gravity was judged dispensable for egg development but needed for normal larvae.

61.manipulation: Measured middle- and hind-leg tibiae on exuviae and imagines preserved since the 1906 regeneration experiments, comparing regenerating legs after amputation or autotomy with normal legs.
61.design: Retrospective measurement of dry-preserved exuviae: regenerating legs compared with the opposite leg and with 29 normal animals; regeneration course fitted by a formula.
61.readout: Tibia length at each moult; growth quotients from moult to moult for regenerating and normal tibiae.
61.n: 56 mantises: 29 normal controls and 13 regenerating leg series (5 middle-leg, 8 hind-leg).
61.finding: Normal tibiae grew about 1.26-fold per moult; regenerating tibiae grew much faster, slowing to about 1.26 once they matched the opposite leg, and more slowly after later loss.

68.manipulation: Commemorates the life and work of the BVA researcher Dr. Franz Megusar.
68.readout: An account of Megusar's career and contributions.
68.finding: Records that Megušar was killed in action in Volhynia in August 1916; names his work on regeneration and colour change in arthropods, especially jumping-leg regeneration and bleaching of blinded crustaceans.

75.manipulation: Measured rat tail length and analysed it as a facultative sex character.
75.design: Tail length compared between the sexes (and against temperature).
75.finding: In albino brown rats, females had relatively longer tails than males at all ages and temperatures, less so in warmth, ascribed to warmer female bodies; wild agouti rats differed inconsistently.

76.manipulation: Bred temperature-modified rats and measured the tail length of their offspring.
76.design: Offspring tail length of temperature-modified parents versus controls.
76.readout: Whether the parents' temperature-induced tail change appears in offspring.
76.finding: Rats moved 10 °C warmer or colder overshot the new temperature norm for tail length; moved back, they overshot in reverse, then regressed over time; ascribed to transmitted metabolic attunement.

77.manipulation: Measured how the relative tail length increases and computed its temperature coefficient in rats.
77.design: Relative tail-length growth across temperatures, expressed as a temperature quotient.
77.readout: Relative tail length and its Q10.
77.finding: Relative tail growth, related to body rather than air temperature, gave Q10 values averaging about 2, as the reaction-velocity rule predicts; the same held for sex differences, transfers and antipyretics.

80.manipulation: Determined when DOPA appears during the formation of the cocoons of the pine sawfly Lophyrus pini.
80.design: Timing of the DOPA (melanin-precursor) reaction across cocoon formation.
80.readout: The developmental moment at which DOPA is present.
80.n: Lophyrus pini larvae before, during and after spinning, pupae and cocoons
80.finding: The DOPA reaction is absent in feeding larvae and their blood, present in all parts of spinning larvae, then found only in the cocoon, not in larva or pupa.

87.manipulation: Compared the chamber progression of foraminifera with the moulting progression of mantids as parallel growth series.
87.design: Analysis of two growth series under a common geometric law.
87.readout: The progression (ratio series) of foraminiferan chambers and mantid moults.
87.n: Published data: 8 chamber series of 6 species (58 quotients); shell thickness from 35 figures (146 quotients).
87.finding: Foraminiferan shell-chamber growth follows a progression analogous to the mantid moulting series — a shared quantitative growth law across distant taxa.

89.manipulation: Kept freshwater crabs in magnesium-salt solutions (with or without NaCl, warm or cool room, three body sizes), then returned some to tap water; eels kept in seawater.
89.design: Repeated blood samples from treated and tap-water control crabs tested with a microchemical magnesium reaction, first validated on salt solutions and on marine and freshwater crustacean blood.
89.readout: Crystal tufts formed by blood with sodium phosphate, scored as present, doubtful or absent over days to weeks.
89.quantification: Semi-quantitative (+/?/– scoring of the crystal reaction)
89.n: 45 Telphusa crabs (10 troughs in the main series); three eels; blood of five marine and four freshwater or land crustacean species for the method.
89.finding: Magnesium reached crab blood only after about three weeks, faster in small crabs and without NaCl, and left slowly; no experiment yet showed foreign substances reaching the germ-plasm.

90.manipulation: Crossed Japanese waltzing mice with European mice and followed the inheritance of their traits.
90.design: Breeding crosses analysed for trait transmission (notably the waltzing behaviour).
90.readout: Phenotypes and behaviour of the offspring.
90.finding: Waltzing, albinism and spotting segregated as recessives, with runners to waltzers 4.57:1 and too few spotted mice; a malformed litter sired by a male that lost a leg never recurred.

95.manipulation: Placed photographic paper under excised skin and in sealed tubes implanted over the gonads of living fire salamanders, then exposed them to daylight or electric light.
95.design: Light-exposed preparations and animals versus dark-kept controls; blackening compared with a calibrated paper scale (Bunsen–Roscoe law) to compute a penetration coefficient.
95.readout: Blackening of the paper beneath skin, muscle and peritoneum; fraction of incident light transmitted; yellow versus black skin.
95.n: Over 50 operated salamanders with implanted tubes; over 100 penetration determinations; excised skin preparations
95.finding: Šećerov reported about 1/173 of incident light (1/30–1/330) passing the body wall to the gonads, 3–4 times more under yellow than black skin, enough possibly to alter germ cells.

101.manipulation: Cut off whole antennae at the base, or cut antennae at twelve positions (a third and halfway along each segment) in Porcellio scaber; some animals kept at 30 °C.
101.readout: Autotomy site, white wound cone, moult, time to regeneration, and length and pigment of the regenerate.
101.n: 20 animals with whole antennae removed and 24 cut at twelve positions (two per position); nearly 100 amputations in all
101.finding: Two preformed autotomy sites (antennal base; segments 3–4 joint); regeneration also from non-autotomy cut sites; regenerates emerged at the next moult a third shorter, sooner when warm and young.

102.manipulation: Measured the heat-coagulation point of specific muscle plasmas and tested its dependence on the animal's living temperature.
102.design: Coagulation temperature of muscle proteins from animals living at different temperatures.
102.readout: The coagulation point of muscle plasma.
102.n: 11 species surveyed; 10 each of water frogs, toads and fire salamanders heat-kept, muscle tested in 2 salamanders, 1 frog and 2 toads; hibernating tortoises and bat.
102.finding: The coagulation point of muscle plasma is independent of the temperature the animal lived at — a fixed biochemical property.

103.manipulation: Gradually transferred freshwater fishes to salt water to test their adaptation.
103.design: Survival and condition across increasing salinity.
103.readout: Survival and condition at each salinity; freezing-point depression of blood compared with the medium; body ash after magnesium-salt exposure.
103.quantification: Quantitative (freezing-point depression of blood and medium)
103.finding: Lamprey larvae, sterlet, carp and pike tolerated salt only to a freezing point near −1.0 °C, blood equilibrating with the medium (gills salt-permeable); eel gills judged impermeable.

104.manipulation: Removed hermit crabs from their shells and observed how the abdomen differentiates.
104.design: De-shelled animals of five species kept shell-free through one or more moults and compared with the shelled state; one series kept in darkness versus light.
104.readout: Differentiation and form of the (normally asymmetric, soft) abdomen.
104.n: 72 de-shelled animals: 40 Eupagurus (four species), 20 Diogenes varians, 12 E. prideauxii in darkness (5) or light (7); many died before moulting.
104.finding: Moulting without shells made the abdomen segmented, tougher, shorter and flatter, and pigmented in Eupagurus even in darkness; appendage and claw asymmetry unchanged; normal form attributed to shell pressure.

105.manipulation: No new experiment: reports malformed regenerates that arose in earlier regeneration experiments on lobsters at Trieste and on a praying mantis, and their loss.
105.design: Case reports of two lobster claws and one mantis foreleg, compared with daphnid ‘preliminary regenerates’ from 1896–98, with a theoretical argument against Bordage.
105.readout: Dates of loss, size of the malformed regenerate, whether it was shed by autotomy or left in the moult, and later regrowth.
105.n: Three cases: two lobster claw regenerates and one triplicated mantis foreleg
105.finding: Two malformed lobster claws were shed by autotomy without a moult, one then regrown normally; a triplicated mantis foreleg stayed in the moult; Przibram inferred a regulation needing no selection.

113.manipulation: Enforced colour changes and bred the animals to test whether the changes are inherited (reptile material).
113.design: Offspring of colour-modified animals versus controls.
113.readout: Whether the enforced colour change reappears in offspring.
113.finding: Kammerer reported inheritance of experimentally enforced colour changes (a neo-Lamarckian claim, later disputed).

118.manipulation: Cut off the anterior or posterior end of young Clepsine tessulata (3–3½ mm, taken from the mother) and followed regeneration for 23 days.
118.design: Regeneration of anterior versus posterior ends.
118.readout: Rebuilding of head and tail ends.
118.n: 40 young leeches: 20 with the anterior and 20 with the posterior end removed
118.finding: After 23 days there were 3 complete and 5 incomplete anterior regenerates (of 20) and 2 incomplete posterior ones (of 20); the author concluded leeches are no exception among annelids.

120.manipulation: Kept alga-covered and alga-free larvae in carbonated, overcrowded, fouled or soapy water, with Saprolegnia, or in darkness; transferred algae between larvae; cultured algae on other substrates.
120.design: Paired glasses of alga-covered versus alga-free larvae of the same species under each condition, several trials repeated; field observations at a single laundry pond.
120.readout: Larval survival over days, water turbidity, algal persistence and regrowth after moults, success of algal transfer and culture.
120.quantification: Semi-quantitative (survival counts in groups of 3–12 larvae)
120.finding: Kammerer reported a mutualism: in light the algae helped larvae survive carbonated, fouled or soapy water and Saprolegnia; in darkness the advantage reversed; the alga grew best on larvae.

121.manipulation: Removed and followed the regeneration of secondary sexual characters in amphibians.
121.design: Regeneration of secondary sex characters (e.g., breeding crest, thumb pads).
121.readout: Whether and how the secondary sex characters regrow.
121.n: About 14 frog, toad and newt taxa; animal numbers given for only a few series
121.finding: Male nuptial pads, vocal sacs, newt crests, lip and toe lobes, tail filaments and spurs regenerated, often first simplified or juvenile-like; crest changes spread to uninjured neighbouring crest.

122.manipulation: Cut or pressed off the second antennae or the furca and caudal setae of sexually mature Cyclops and of juveniles after their second moult.
122.design: Seven groups: broods from ten isolated females with moult records; antenna and furca amputations in adults and juveniles; unoperated adult and juvenile controls.
122.readout: Moults, clot or regeneration bud, and regenerated antennal segments or caudal setae; moult dates from hatching to sexual maturity.
122.n: 50 adults (antennae) and over 100 (furca); about 50 juveniles (antennae) and over 120 (furca); moult records for 100 young; 20 adult controls
122.finding: Cyclops reached sexual maturity at the sixth moult and never moulted again; adults formed only a clot, while some juveniles regenerated antennal segments or caudal setae at the next moult.

123.manipulation: Removed the tentacle and eye of the pond snail Limnaea stagnalis and followed their regeneration.
123.design: Observation of tentacle and eye regeneration.
123.readout: Rebuilding of the tentacle and its eye.
123.n: Four snails, one per operation type (tentacle tips, distal piece, tentacle with eye, whole tentacle with eye and surrounding skin)
123.finding: The pond snail regenerates its tentacle together with the eye it carries.

124.manipulation: Removed the caudal horn of the silkworm caterpillar Bombyx mori and followed its regeneration.
124.readout: Whether and how the caudal horn regrows.
124.n: 20 larvae operated three days after hatching; 3 survived an epidemic; 1 preserved with a regenerate
124.finding: A horn cut off three days after hatching regrew smaller (1 mm against 1.5 mm) and less bristly in the one larva preserved; Kellogg’s older larvae had not regrown it.

126.manipulation: Removed lung tissue in the fire salamander and other amphibians and followed its regeneration.
126.design: Observation of lung regeneration across amphibians.
126.readout: Whether and how lung tissue regrows.
126.n: 66–70 salamanders (40 cut without ligature, all failed; 26 ligated, 16 survived), 14 Triton cristatus, 2 Rana esculenta, 2 Bufo vulgaris
126.finding: Salamandra, Rana and Bufo lungs regenerate after partial or complete removal when ligated before cutting, via an epithelial regeneration bud; the intact lung hypertrophies; Triton undecided.

136.manipulation: Placed photographic paper in tubes beside the gonads of anaesthetized lizards and under skin preparations, exposed to lamps and sunlight; examined peritoneal pigment in day- and night-active lizards.
136.design: Light penetration through the body wall of Lacerta viridis and L. serpa measured by zone against a graded exposure scale and compared with Salamandra; comparative survey of peritoneal pigmentation.
136.readout: Blackening of photographic paper against exposure-scale papers, converted to a light-penetration coefficient; presence or absence of black peritoneal pigment.
136.n: Seven tube measurements in L. viridis plus photograms of skin preparations; peritoneum of seven lizard species, six more geckos added in a printing note.
136.finding: About 1/4,500 of incident light passed the belly wall and 1/202,500 the unpigmented back, far less than in Salamandra; pigmented peritoneum, lacking in night geckos, probably shields the interior.

137.manipulation: Induced tail-skin autotomy by clamping or lifting dormice by the tail, or cut tails with bone shears (young edible dormice, opossums, a kangaroo, rats).
137.design: Tails measured before and after; stumps followed for up to 14 months, with X-rays and histology of the vertebral end.
137.readout: Wound closure, regrowth and colour of the hair tuft, and lengthening of the last tail vertebra.
137.n: 9 hazel, 8 garden and 9 edible dormice, 4 brown rats, 3 opossums, 2 kangaroos (not all operated), plus three young edible dormice
137.finding: Tail skin autotomizes and no tail regrows; the stump closes, grows a new, often darker hair tuft, and the broken last vertebra may lengthen into a bony stub.

139.manipulation: Measured whether the size of freshly hatched mantises increases with the mother's age.
139.design: Hatchling size as a function of maternal age (a test of Halban's maternal-age effect).
139.readout: Size of newly hatched mantises across maternal ages.
139.n: 455 hatchlings from 10 oothecae of 3 once-mated females (about 50 per ootheca, 15 in one).
139.finding: Freshly hatched mantises do NOT increase in size with the mother's age — a negative result for the maternal-age effect in this species.

142.manipulation: Painted pupation-ready caterpillars’ eyes black, yellow or blue; kept them at graded yellow intensities, in neutral light or under opposite-coloured bells; set others on Hering and Ostwald papers.
142.design: Black-painted versus normal eyes across yellow intensities; yellow or blue lacquered eyes in neutral light and under opposite-coloured bells, with unlacquered controls; coloured papers versus equally bright greys.
142.readout: Pupal colour type (gold, gold-green, middle or dark) counted per condition.
142.finding: Pupae mostly followed the colour of lacquer on the eyes, even under opposite-coloured light; yellow papers gave gold pupae, equally bright greys did not: colour acts through the eye.

144.manipulation: Transplanted the spleen in adult urodeles and followed the graft.
144.design: Observation of spleen-graft survival and behaviour.
144.readout: Survival and condition of the transplanted spleen.
144.n: 36 newts: 25 spleen exchanges (23 T. cristatus, 2 T. alpestris; 3 died early), 4 splenectomies, 4 second-spleen implants, 3 autoplastic replants
144.finding: Spleens exchanged between newts without vascular sutures healed in, vascularised and kept normal histology with mitoses for up to 122 days in 9 of 25; removed spleens did not regenerate.

151.manipulation: Excised four ribs in adult newts (series I), or ribs with the overlying skin, muscle and yellow spots (series II), and followed the spots or the regenerating skin.
151.design: Two operative series on adults, observed for up to five months: rib removal leaving the spots in place; removal of ribs together with the spotted skin.
151.readout: Colour of the yellow lateral spots after rib removal; appearance of yellow spots in regenerated skin.
151.n: Not stated; four ribs removed per animal.
151.finding: Yellow spots kept their colour five months after rib removal and appeared in regenerated skin without ribs; the pigment forms independently of rib pressure.

152.manipulation: Injected half a litter with tuberculin to induce fever (none resulted); the whole litter, whose parents had come from a cold cellar into the heated laboratory, ran warm; repeated once.
152.design: Body temperature and body:tail ratio of the warm litter over 10 days compared with published norms (Bierens de Haan temperatures, Donaldson growth tables); injected versus uninjected littermates.
152.readout: Tail length as a function of raised body temperature.
152.finding: Rats running over 1 °C above normal body temperature grew relatively longer tails than published norms; tuberculin gave no fever; the authors ascribed tail length to body heat.

155.manipulation: None; described five wild-caught beetles with abnormal antennae from the institute museum, three with tarsus-like segments.
155.design: Descriptive comparison of two ordinary antennal regenerates with three tarsus-like cases, using injury traces to infer regenerative origin.
155.readout: Segment number, hairs, end segment and leg-like features of each abnormal antenna; injury traces elsewhere on the body.
155.finding: Interpreted tarsus-like antennal segments on three wild beetles as heteromorphic regenerates (one substitutive, two accessory) and rejected ganglionic control, proposing a twofold potency in each appendage.

162.manipulation: Described the spontaneous formation of a second lens (lentoid) in the eye of a catfish.
162.design: Histological description of a developmental anomaly.
162.readout: Structure and position of the spontaneous second lens.
162.n: One eye of a single wels catfish, about 20 cm long
162.finding: Documents a spontaneously formed second lens in a fish eye — a natural lentoid bearing on lens formation and regeneration.

163.manipulation: No experiment: examined one carp pharyngeal bone whose largest grinding tooth was displaced out of the chewing plane; cited his earlier dark-rearing of a hawk moth.
163.design: Argument from cases judged probable (innate spatial orientation, pre-formed calluses, embryonic grinding teeth), plus anatomical comparison of the displaced and normal teeth in section.
163.readout: Whether a tooth that could never have chewed nonetheless bore a grinding surface.
163.n: One malformed carp pharyngeal bone; other cases from the literature.
163.finding: The displaced tooth, which could never have chewed, still bore a grinding surface; Demoll concluded that carp grinding teeth are largely inherited individual acquisitions.

166.manipulation: Measured and described, bone by bone, the macerated skeleton of one intersex adult (testes, female-type external genitalia).
166.design: Single-case osteometric description, judged against male and female norms and compared with published skeletons of intersex people.
166.readout: Skeletal structure of the partial hermaphrodite.
166.finding: The skeleton combined male and female traits, with unusually long limb bones and many anomalies; Stieve linked the mixed traits and long bones to disturbed gonadal internal secretion.

173.manipulation: Tested whether the female cycle and pregnancy of rats depend on temperature.
173.design: Female reproductive cycle and gestation across temperatures.
173.readout: Timing of the cycle and pregnancy under varied temperature.
173.finding: Litter-to-litter intervals (mean 24 days) showed no trend with rearing temperature from 5 to 40 °C; Przibram ascribed this to a secondary homoiothermy of females in heat and pregnancy.

175.manipulation: Summarised, in a one-page review, the rule proposed by the physicist Karl Przibram linking the propagation or growth velocity of a structure to its form.
175.design: Review (Referat) of a 1920 paper in Die Naturwissenschaften, with biological examples; no experiments or data.
175.readout: The proposed link between form and rate of growth.
175.finding: Reports the rule of Karl Przibram: faster propagation or growth yields elongated, finely branched forms, slower growth compact ones; examples include etiolation, Daphnia helmets and long tails of warm-reared mice.
